articles.title: # A failed Playwright test is not a diagnosis
articles.excerpt: Your Playwright test failed. The build is red. A notification arrives. Someone opens the report. And then the real work begins. Was this a product bug? A flaky test? A selector that changed? Missing t…
articles.body: Your Playwright test failed. The build is red. A notification arrives. Someone opens the report. And then the real work begins. Was this a product bug? A flaky test? A selector that changed? Missing test data? An environment issue? Or simply a report with too little context? For many teams, test execution is already automated. Understanding the result is not. The 5 questions to answer after a failed run 1. Can we identify the exact run? Capture the essentials before discussing the failure: Test name Browser and environment Commit or build reference Execution time The system or person that triggered the run Without this context, a red result is difficult to reproduce and easy to misinterpret. 2. Is the failure reproducible? One failed run is evidence, not yet a diagnosis.

articles.title: Context drift: when a multi-agent crew's shared beliefs about the goal go stale
articles.excerpt: Originally published on Loop & Retry — field notes on building LLM agents that survive production. A cache that's never invalidated doesn't know it's wrong. It read a value once, the value was correct…
articles.body: Originally published on Loop & Retry — field notes on building LLM agents that survive production. A cache that's never invalidated doesn't know it's wrong. It read a value once, the value was correct at the moment it was read, and it will keep serving that exact value — confidently, correctly-looking, forever — even after the source of truth moved on without telling it. The context window is a cache : the same staleness that degrades one agent's working memory over a long run degrades a whole crew's shared understanding of what it's even trying to do, except a crew has more places for a stale copy to sit unnoticed.

articles.title: Roundtables: A Conversation With the Creator of AI-Designed Viruses
articles.excerpt: Friday, October 16, 2026 Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blue…
articles.body: Friday, October 16, 2026 Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next. Join senior AI reporter James O’Donnell as he interviews King about his work, being named one of MIT Technology Review’s Innovators Under 35 and new ways of seeing biology. Going live on October 16th at 18:30 BST / 1:30pm EDT / 10:30am PDT Register now Speakers : James O’Donnell , AI Reporter, and Samuel King , Bioengineering PhD Candidate, Stanford University/Arc Institute Related Stories He asked an AI to design viruses … and it worked.
